statements.explainer: Zoning rules decide how many homes can be built and how tall. Requiring more density tends to lower prices over time and reduce sprawl; some residents object to the change in their neighbourhoods and the strain on pipes and roads.

national.evidence: Wants to "free up land, streamline planning and consenting, and finance the infrastructure needed for development" (Salient guide); removing the ban on minimum car-parking is the only partial exception.

green.evidence: Encourage mixed-use areas and walkability in new housing developments.

act.evidence: Favours increasing supply through deregulation and easier consenting (Salient guide).

opportunity.evidence: Revamp zoning to reduce house prices.

statements.text: Everyone should get some free GP visits each year, paid for by the government.
statements.explainer: Most adults currently pay $20 to $80 or more per GP visit. Free visits would remove a cost barrier to seeing a doctor but would need hundreds of millions of dollars a year and more GPs to meet demand.

national.evidence: Says Labour's "free" promises (including the Medicard) total $18 billion and would need "nine new taxes"; offers rural doctor funding and pharmacist access instead.

labour.evidence: Make up to three GP visits a year free with a Medicard.

green.evidence: Increase free public health services.

alliance.evidence: "Elimination of costs for GP visits, dental, optical, and audiology services."

statements.text: The $5 charge for each prescription should be scrapped for everyone.
statements.explainer: Most adults pay $5 per prescription item, with exemptions for children, Community Services Card holders and over-65s. Removing it for everyone costs roughly $150 million a year; supporters say it stops people skipping medicines, opponents say the money is better targeted.

national.evidence: Keeps the $5 charge it reinstated in 2024 for most adults, with "targeted free prescriptions to seniors" instead of universal free prescriptions.

labour.evidence: Remove the $5 charge for prescriptions (restore universal free prescriptions).

statements.text: Free school lunches should be expanded and made more generous, even if it costs more.
statements.explainer: Schools in poorer areas get a free lunch programme funded at roughly $3 a meal. Expanding it to more schools or spending more per meal costs more each year; supporters point to attendance and learning, opponents to cost and food waste.

labour.evidence: Pay for school lunches that cost $5 per meal and ensure schools provide locally made lunches.

green.evidence: Keep and expand the free school lunches programme.

opportunity.evidence: Rebuild the school lunch programme.

statements.text: Privately run but publicly funded schools (charter schools) should continue to be allowed alongside state schools.
statements.explainer: Charter schools receive government funding per student but are run by private operators with more freedom over curriculum, hours and teacher pay, and less direct oversight. Supporters say they give choice to families poorly served by state schools; opponents say they divert money and lack accountability.

labour.evidence: Labour vowed in 2024 to "get rid of" charter schools if returned to government.

green.evidence: Green alternative Budget 2025 includes "Abolition of Charter Schools Agency".

act.evidence: ACT campaigns on expanding charter schools.

statements.text: University and polytechnic study should be fees-free.
statements.explainer: Students currently borrow fees through the student loan scheme, with limited fees-free support. Making study free costs the government more each year and mostly benefits those who go on to tertiary study; supporters say it widens access and reduces debt.

national.evidence: National's student policy is lowering the student-loan repayment rate to 10%, not fees-free study.

labour.evidence: Labour's 2026 student offer is a 10% student-loan cut for graduates who did not get Fees Free, not a return to fees-free study.

green.evidence: Introduce fees-free tertiary education, universal student allowances and paid placements.

alliance.evidence: Platform promises "free education and healthcare" (RNZ summary of the Alliance).

statements.text: Anyone convicted of a third serious violent or sexual offence should get a mandatory longer sentence, with little room for the judge to decide otherwise.
statements.explainer: Mandatory sentencing laws set minimum penalties for repeat offenders. Supporters say they keep dangerous people off the streets and deter crime; critics say they fill prisons, remove judges' discretion and can lead to harsh results in unusual cases.

national.evidence: Voted for the Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Act 2024 at every reading.

labour.evidence: Voted against reinstatement; justice spokesperson Duncan Webb said three-strikes regimes did little to reduce serious crime.

green.evidence: Voted against; Tamatha Paul said it would disproportionately target Māori and increase incarceration.

act.evidence: Voted for reinstating three strikes; 2026 policy adds a minimum three-year sentence for a third burglary conviction.

nz-first.evidence: Voted for the Reinstating Three Strikes Amendment Act 2024.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Voted against the Reinstating Three Strikes Bill.

alliance.evidence: Justice policy reframes it as "Three strikes and into treatment" — prevention and rehabilitation rather than longer sentences.

conservative.evidence: Wants "meaningful consequences for serious and repeat offending" and longer sentences for repeat child sex offenders.

statements.text: We should send fewer people to prison and put more into rehabilitation and community-based sentences.
statements.explainer: New Zealand imprisons more people per head than most comparable countries. Community sentences and rehabilitation cost less per person and may reduce reoffending; opponents say they are too lenient and put victims at risk.

national.evidence: Add 240 beds to Christchurch Men's Prison; backs tougher sentencing (three strikes).

green.evidence: Prioritise rehabilitation for convicted offenders; reduce restrictions on judges' decisions.

act.evidence: Tougher sentencing, including a mandatory minimum for a third burglary conviction.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Abolish prisons by 2040 and move towards restorative justice.

opportunity.evidence: Boost court and rehabilitation funding to reduce reoffending.

legalise-cannabis.evidence: "Education not incarceration" — redirect money from prohibition enforcement to health and education.

alliance.evidence: "Three strikes and into treatment. Prevent harm, rehabilitate, support victims."

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: "Prison Sinking Lid Policy" — shift non-violent offenders with addiction and mental-health needs out of prison into localised rehabilitation.

statements.text: Farmers should pay for their greenhouse gas emissions, for example by bringing agriculture into the Emissions Trading Scheme.
statements.explainer: Agriculture produces about half of New Zealand's emissions but, unlike other sectors, does not pay for them. Pricing them encourages lower-emission farming and helps meet climate targets; farmers say it would cut production and send farming offshore.

national.evidence: Maintain the current position of agricultural emissions not being priced or offset through the ETS.

labour.evidence: Made no commitment to price farm emissions: "in government Labour will urgently review the ETS" (Greenpeace survey answer).

green.evidence: "We will bring agricultural emissions into the ETS" (answer to Greenpeace 2026 survey).

act.evidence: Ensure agriculture is not part of the emissions trading scheme.

nz-first.evidence: "No, NZ First does not support emissions pricing in any form unless adopted by key trading partners" (Greenpeace survey).

te-pati-maori.evidence: Answered "Yes" to bringing agriculture into the ETS by mid-2027 (Greenpeace 2026 survey).

opportunity.evidence: Strengthen the ETS and include agriculture; told Greenpeace it "will explore a cap-and-trade market or novel levy structure" for biogenic methane.

animal-justice.evidence: Wants to "redirect funds away from animal agriculture, through taxes" and transition farmers to plant-based agriculture.

alliance.evidence: Replace the ETS with a carbon tax on a polluter-pays principle (no specific farm carve-out stated).

conservative.evidence: "There is no climate emergency... Laws/agreements like the Paris Accord, Zero Carbon Act, and Emissions Trading Scheme impose significant costs."

statements.text: New Zealand should keep its legal target of net-zero emissions by 2050 and stay in the Paris climate agreement.
statements.explainer: The 2050 target is written into law and the Paris agreement commits the country to international emissions pledges. Keeping them means ongoing costs and regulation; leaving or weakening them risks trade and reputational consequences.

labour.evidence: "Labour is fully committed to the Paris Agreement and will put New Zealand on course to meet its targets."

green.evidence: Enforce timely implementation of climate legislation and increase Zero Carbon Act reporting and transparency.

act.evidence: Repeal the Zero Carbon Act and NZ's net-zero goal.

nz-first.evidence: Says it would withdraw New Zealand from the Paris Agreement (Salient guide; KPMG tracker: "Campaigned to leave the Paris Accord").

opportunity.evidence: Retain the Climate Change Commission and ensure NZ's emissions goals align with the Paris Agreement.

nz-loyal.evidence: "End climate accords based on faulty science" (party website as quoted by RNZ).

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: "Let's get out of Paris accord and work for solutions to mitigate weather risks."

conservative.evidence: "New Zealand should leave the Paris Agreement"; all climate legislation "should be repealed or withdrawn".

vision-nz.evidence: "Restore absolute national sovereignty by leaving the United Nations and the Paris Accord."

statements.text: Ministers should be able to approve big infrastructure, mining and development projects through a faster process that bypasses the normal environmental consent system.
statements.explainer: Normally projects need resource consents, with public input and the right to object. A fast-track lets selected projects be decided by expert panels or ministers in months rather than years; supporters say it gets things built, opponents say it cuts out communities and environmental checks.

national.evidence: Passed the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 (supported at every reading) and proposes a fast-track policy statement for mining.

labour.evidence: Voted against the Act; "Labour will fix the Fast-track Approvals Act so that environmental protections are not overridden, there is public participation" (keeps a fast-track, but changed).

green.evidence: Repeal the Fast-track Approvals Act.

act.evidence: Supported the Fast-track Approvals Act at every reading.

nz-first.evidence: The Act was part of NZ First's coalition agreement; supported at every reading.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Voted against the Fast-track Approvals Act at all three readings.

opportunity.evidence: Answered "Yes" to restoring strong environmental protections and public participation in all resource consenting (Greenpeace survey).

alliance.evidence: Criticises the government for "fast-tracking legislation and using urgency for policies that harm Aotearoa New Zealand".

statements.text: Seabed mining should be banned in New Zealand waters.
statements.explainer: Companies want to mine iron sands and other minerals from the seafloor. A ban protects marine ecosystems and fisheries but forgoes export income and jobs in the regions involved.

national.evidence: Voted against members' bills to ban seabed mining (2023) and created the fast-track pathway used by seabed miners (Greenpeace assessment).

labour.evidence: Answered "Yes" to banning seabed mining (Greenpeace 2026 survey).

green.evidence: Answered "Yes" to banning seabed mining (Greenpeace 2026 survey).

act.evidence: Voted against seabed-mining ban bills (2023); vocal pro-mining stance (Greenpeace assessment).

nz-first.evidence: "No, NZ First does not support a ban; instead, we advocate for higher government levies on minerals extracted from coastal seabed iron sands."

te-pati-maori.evidence: Ban seabed mining.

opportunity.evidence: Permanently ban seabed mining in NZ waters.

animal-justice.evidence: Key objective: "Restrict seabed mining" (restriction rather than outright ban).

statements.text: New offshore oil and gas exploration should be banned again.
statements.explainer: A ban on new offshore exploration permits was in place for several years and has since been lifted. Reinstating it supports the move away from fossil fuels; opponents say it worsens gas shortages and pushes up power prices.

national.evidence: Voted to repeal the ban (Crown Minerals Amendment Act 2025).

labour.evidence: Answered "Yes" to bringing back the ban (Greenpeace survey); Hipkins has said Labour would reinstate it while honouring existing permits.

green.evidence: "Yes. The Green Party wants to see new fossil fuel extraction ended in Aotearoa."

act.evidence: Voted to repeal the ban (Crown Minerals Amendment Act 2025).

nz-first.evidence: "No. NZ First does not support reinstating a blanket ban on oil and gas exploration."

te-pati-maori.evidence: Answered "Yes" to reinstating the ban (Greenpeace survey).

opportunity.evidence: Would "not oppose a reinstatement" but considers it "probably unnecessary" and would not progress it itself.

nz-loyal.evidence: "Establish energy independence, including oil and gas" (party website as quoted by RNZ).

animal-justice.evidence: "Reverse the lifting of the offshore exploration ban and reinstate the moratorium on new fossil fuel permits."

conservative.evidence: "Actively encourage commercial oil and gas exploration."

statements.text: The government should take a bigger direct role in electricity, such as setting up a new state-owned power company or splitting the big power companies into separate generators and retailers.
statements.explainer: Four large companies both generate and sell most of New Zealand's electricity. Breaking them up or adding a state competitor aims to lower prices; opponents say it would deter the investment needed for new generation.

national.evidence: The National-led government's 2025 electricity review response did not include structural separation; Nicola Willis argued splitting the gentailers risked "massive instability".

green.evidence: Establish a publicly owned Crown entity ("Kiwipower") to invest in renewable generation.

act.evidence: Open power transmission to private investment; opposes break-ups and state-run alternatives.

nz-first.evidence: Divide the "generation" and "retail" arms of power companies.

opportunity.evidence: Restructure the electricity market to bring prices down; use the Crown's gentailer stakes to fund renewables.

alliance.evidence: "100 percent public ownership of electricity generation, transmission, distribution, and retail."

statements.text: Parliament should write a single legal definition of the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi, rather than leaving the courts and the Waitangi Tribunal to interpret them case by case.
statements.explainer: The Treaty's "principles" are referred to in many laws but defined by courts and the Tribunal over time. Fixing them in statute would give Parliament the final say and could narrow Māori rights as currently understood; opponents say it rewrites a founding agreement without Māori consent.

national.evidence: Voted against the Bill at its second reading after supporting it only to select committee; Luxon pledged to refuse a Treaty referendum.

labour.evidence: Voted against at both readings; said the Bill's principles "did not match the principles of the Treaty".

green.evidence: Voted against at both readings.

act.evidence: Sponsored the Treaty Principles Bill; its 11 MPs were the only votes in favour at the second reading (10 April 2025).

nz-first.evidence: Voted against at the second reading, but its own policy is to remove references to "the principles of the Treaty" from legislation.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Voted against at both readings; MPs led the haka protest at the first reading.

statements.text: The Waitangi Tribunal should be abolished or replaced once historical claims are settled.
statements.explainer: The Tribunal investigates Crown breaches of the Treaty and makes mostly non-binding recommendations on both historical and current issues. Winding it up would end an independent check on government; supporters say its job is done once settlements finish.

green.evidence: Implement Waitangi Tribunal recommendations; uphold te Tiriti across government decision-making.

act.evidence: Abolish the Waitangi Tribunal once historical claims are resolved.

nz-first.evidence: Replace the Waitangi Tribunal with a Treaty of Waitangi Completion Commission.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Make Waitangi Tribunal recommendations binding.

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: Increase and entrench Waitangi Tribunal funding and extend its binding jurisdiction on the Crown.

statements.text: The Māori electorates should be abolished, or their future put to a referendum.
statements.explainer: Seven seats in Parliament are elected by voters on the Māori roll, guaranteeing Māori representation. Abolishing them, or asking all voters to decide, is argued as treating everyone the same; opponents say only Māori should decide the future of their seats.

green.evidence: Entrench the Māori electoral seats.

nz-first.evidence: Introduce a binding referendum on the Māori seats.

statements.text: Public services such as health should be targeted by need alone, with no programmes aimed specifically at Māori or other ethnic groups.
statements.explainer: Māori have worse outcomes on many measures. One view is that Māori-led or ethnicity-targeted services close those gaps faster; the other is that help should go to whoever needs it most regardless of ethnicity.

labour.evidence: Introduce a Māori-led job training programme and fund; allocate 5% of government procurement to Māori businesses.

green.evidence: Simplify funding for Hauora Māori providers; create a Māori Education Authority.

act.evidence: Remove ethnicity-based criteria for delivering public services.

nz-first.evidence: Disestablish the Independent Māori Statutory Board from Auckland Council; policy is to remove "principles of the Treaty" references from environmental laws.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Invest in Māori health outcomes; Māori-led health, education, disability and justice systems.

nz-loyal.evidence: "Scrap all race-based policies" (party website as quoted by RNZ).

alliance.evidence: Māori health providers keep the option to remain independent with full funding; constitutional change with Te Tiriti at the centre.

conservative.evidence: "Employment, promotion and access to public services should be based on individual need, ability and merit."

vision-nz.evidence: "Completely remove all race-based targeted policies and spending within the healthcare sector"; "End all race-based politics."

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: "Te Aka Motuhake" — an autonomous, state-funded, iwi-governed Māori health authority.

statements.text: A recent law that requires every new piece of legislation to be checked against a fixed list of "good regulation" principles, including protecting private property rights, should be scrapped.
statements.explainer: The law sets up a board to report on whether new laws meet principles such as the rule of law, protection of property and compensation when rules reduce property values. Supporters say it stops bad regulation; opponents say it privileges property owners over the environment and the Treaty and lets an unelected board second-guess Parliament.

national.evidence: Voted for the Bill at all three readings; did not answer Greenpeace's repeal question.

labour.evidence: Lodged a member's bill to repeal it (Nov 2025); "Yes" to repealing it in the Greenpeace survey.

green.evidence: "Yes" to repealing the Regulatory Standards Act (Greenpeace survey).

act.evidence: Wrote and sponsored the Act (David Seymour, Minister for Regulation).

nz-first.evidence: Mixed: voted for it in 2025, Winston Peters then said NZ First would repeal it, but its 2026 Greenpeace survey answer did not commit to repeal.

te-pati-maori.evidence: "Yes" to repealing the Regulatory Standards Act (Greenpeace survey).

opportunity.evidence: "Yes" to repealing the Regulatory Standards Act (Greenpeace survey).

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: "As a matter of priority, vote to repeal both the Regulatory Standards Act 2025 and the Treaty Clauses Review."

statements.text: Political donations should be capped, and only individual New Zealand voters should be allowed to donate.
statements.explainer: There is currently no limit on how much a person can give to a party, and companies, trusts and unions can donate. Caps and a voters-only rule reduce the influence of wealthy donors; opponents say they restrict free participation and favour parties with many small donors.

labour.evidence: No commitment: "Labour believes in transparent and fair rules for political party donations" (Greenpeace survey).

green.evidence: "Yes"; also "capping a donor's donations at a level that does not risk donor influence over policy."

nz-first.evidence: Supports "electoral integrity and transparency" but has no policy restricting donations to voters (Greenpeace survey).

te-pati-maori.evidence: "Yes" to limiting donations to registered voters (Greenpeace survey).

opportunity.evidence: Cap donations at $30,000 per donor per election and ban donations from companies and trusts.

animal-justice.evidence: Committed to "getting money out of politics" (no specific cap stated).

statements.text: Central government should cap how much councils can raise rates each year.
statements.explainer: Rates are the main income for local councils and have been rising well above inflation. A cap protects ratepayers but leaves councils with less money for water pipes, roads and other infrastructure unless they are given other funding tools.

national.evidence: Instruct councils to keep annual rate increases between 2 and 4 percent.

labour.evidence: Mixed: Barbara Edmonds said Labour supported the rates-cap bill to its first reading, while Tangi Utikere said in Dec 2025 "we don't support this rates cap" (both as quoted by National).

green.evidence: Reject the proposed rates cap and allow councils to use more funding tools.

opportunity.evidence: Give councils more tools to invest in infrastructure (rather than limiting revenue).

statements.text: Overall immigration to New Zealand should be reduced.
statements.explainer: Migration adds workers, students and skills but also pressure on housing and infrastructure. Lower immigration eases that pressure; employers say it worsens labour shortages and slows growth.

green.evidence: Increase the refugee quota and support migrant workers to residency.

nz-first.evidence: Replace the Accredited Employer Work Visa with a shortage-led skilled visa; remove automatic student-visa work rights; tie immigration to genuine labour shortages.

conservative.evidence: Cap net immigration of unskilled and semi-skilled workers (zero if social goods are not increasing), while welcoming skilled migrants.

vision-nz.evidence: "Pause mass immigration immediately to review visa policies and relieve pressure on local infrastructure."

statements.text: New residents should have to wait longer (five years or more) before they can get most benefits.
statements.explainer: Most benefits currently require two years' residence. A longer wait saves money and is argued to attract migrants who will not need support; critics say it leaves families with no safety net if they lose work.

national.evidence: Change entitlements for benefits for new NZ residents to five years.

act.evidence: "ACT will introduce a five-year welfare stand-down for residence class visa holders" (2026 Fiscal Plan).

nz-first.evidence: A benefit stand-down period of ten years for migrants, and longer residency for citizenship.

statements.text: The age for receiving NZ Superannuation should stay at 65.
statements.explainer: Super is paid to everyone from 65 regardless of income or wealth. Keeping 65 is the status quo; raising it (for example gradually to 67) saves billions as the population ages but is hardest on people in physical jobs and those with shorter life expectancy.

national.evidence: Would "have liked to make change" and has long backed 67 from a future date, but its 2026 election policy is only to hold cross-party accord talks on the retirement system.

labour.evidence: "Labour has been clear that it will not means test New Zealand superannuation or increase the age of eligibility."

green.evidence: "Yes. We will retain NZ Superannuation as a universal entitlement from age 65."

act.evidence: Raise the retirement age to 67 by 2035 (three months a year).

nz-first.evidence: "New Zealand First will not support changes to the entitlement or eligibility of New Zealand Superannuation."

te-pati-maori.evidence: Says the age of eligibility "should not be raised at all" and should be lower for Māori because of lower life expectancy (May 2023 statement; no newer position found).

opportunity.evidence: Answered "Yes" to retaining the eligibility age at 65 (Grey Power survey).

alliance.evidence: "Keeps the age of entitlement for Super at 65."

statements.text: Main benefits (such as Jobseeker and Sole Parent Support) should be substantially increased.
statements.explainer: Benefit rates are adjusted each year and many recipients are below the poverty line. Larger increases reduce hardship directly but cost more and, some argue, reduce the incentive to work.

national.evidence: Reduce benefit payments for people receiving support for more than two years.

green.evidence: Increase benefit payments and improve standards for beneficiaries.

act.evidence: ACT's 2026 Fiscal Plan has no benefit increases; it tightens eligibility (independent medical certification for health and disability benefits, a five-year stand-down for new residents).

te-pati-maori.evidence: "We will scrap benefit sanctions and ensure everybody is paid enough to live with dignity, whether they are in employment or not" (Oct 2024 press release).

opportunity.evidence: A universal Citizens' Income of up to $370 a week, replacing many main benefits.

alliance.evidence: Proposes a Universal Benefit, individual entitlements, universal child payments and an end to benefit sanctions.

womens-rights.evidence: "Minimum wages and benefits need to be increased so that all people have living incomes."

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: Replace the "complex, punitive benefit system" with a non-taxable Universal Whānau Allowance and wipe MSD/IRD debt for low-income whānau.

statements.text: People on benefits should face tougher obligations and sanctions, such as drug testing or payment cuts if they do not meet requirements.
statements.explainer: Sanctions reduce or suspend payments when obligations such as job-seeking are not met. Supporters say they move people into work; opponents say they punish children and people with health problems and do little to create jobs.

national.evidence: Introduce drug testing for people receiving benefits; reduce payments after two years on a benefit; longer stand-downs.

green.evidence: Increase benefit payments and improve standards for beneficiaries; refuse to use AI for welfare decisions.

act.evidence: Restrict medical certification for health-related benefits and monitor spending of long-term jobseekers.

te-pati-maori.evidence: "We will scrap benefit sanctions"; called the traffic-light sanctions system "a tool designed to punish whānau" (Oct 2024 press release).

opportunity.evidence: Citizen's Income replaces most main benefits: "no Work and Income appointments, no relationship status checks—just a guaranteed payment".

alliance.evidence: "An end to benefit sanctions."

conservative.evidence: "Welfare: Reform is needed. Fifty years of expanding welfare has undermined our families and created an underclass."

vision-nz.evidence: "Dismantle state dependency"; "Slash state dependency by eliminating financial rules that disincentivise marriage."

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: Replace the "punitive benefit system" and end "relationship status" policing.

statements.text: Transport money should go mainly to public transport, cycling and rail rather than new highways.
statements.explainer: The national transport fund is limited, so spending on big new highways competes with buses, trains and cycleways. Roads suit freight and regions; public transport suits cities and reduces emissions and congestion.

national.evidence: Complete construction of the next set of Roads of National Significance; fund the $800m Christchurch Northern Motorway extension.

labour.evidence: Introduce a $20 weekly public-transport fare cap in the main cities ($10 elsewhere).

green.evidence: Build mass rapid transit in three major cities and invest in better rail and bus links; free or $2 fares.

act.evidence: Focus the National Land Transport Fund on road infrastructure only.

nz-first.evidence: Establish a 12-month trial of commuter rail in Canterbury and further south.

opportunity.evidence: Make public transport free.

alliance.evidence: Publicly owned rail and coastal shipping as "twin backbones" of freight, more public-transport funding.

statements.text: Rules limiting farm pollution of rivers (such as limits on nitrogen fertiliser and stock numbers) should be strengthened rather than loosened.
statements.explainer: Many rivers and lakes fail swimming or ecological standards, largely from farm run-off. Tighter rules improve water quality over time but raise costs for farmers; looser rules do the reverse.

national.evidence: Supported blocking regional freshwater plans and let restrictions on intensification lapse (Greenpeace assessment).

labour.evidence: Says "freshwater limits should be national bottom lines" and wants councils able to implement the 2020 freshwater policy, but would not commit to lowering the nitrogen cap.

green.evidence: Impose nitrogen caps on all agricultural practices; phase out synthetic nitrogen fertiliser.

act.evidence: Replace Te Mana o te Wai with measurable freshwater outcomes.

nz-first.evidence: "No. Our approach is for practical, science-based freshwater management that balances environmental outcomes with productive land use."

te-pati-maori.evidence: Answered "Yes" to immediately lowering the synthetic nitrogen fertiliser cap and banning new dairy conversions (Greenpeace survey).

opportunity.evidence: Tighten rules on water quality and reinstate Te Mana o te Wai, but did not back a lower fertiliser cap.

animal-justice.evidence: Links intensive dairying to "degradation of waterways"; seeks to transition away from animal agriculture.

statements.text: Rules on gene technology (genetic modification) should be relaxed so modified crops and organisms can be used outside the laboratory.
statements.explainer: Gene editing is currently effectively confined to the lab. Relaxing the rules could bring faster-growing crops, pest control and medical uses; opponents worry about the environment and about the "GM-free" image of New Zealand exports.

national.evidence: The Gene Technology Bill is a National-led government bill; National remains in favour (it lacks NZ First's votes to pass).

labour.evidence: Withheld support at select committee citing limited consultation and lack of regulatory independence.

green.evidence: Called the Bill a "radical liberalisation and deregulation of GM technology" and withheld support.

act.evidence: Supports the Gene Technology Bill (with objections to its Māori advisory committee).

nz-first.evidence: Would not support the Bill into law without major changes, calling it "far too liberal" and lacking safeguards.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Told RNZ it "remained opposed to the bill".

opportunity.evidence: Rewrite gene technology regulations to enable modern gene technologies.

conservative.evidence: "We oppose the current government's move to end the long-standing restrictions placed on field trials and the release of genetically modified organisms."

statements.text: New Zealand should formally recognise the State of Palestine now.
statements.explainer: Recognition is a diplomatic step many countries, including Australia, Canada and the UK, have taken. Supporters see it as backing a two-state solution; opponents say it should wait for a negotiated settlement.

national.evidence: Government (PM Luxon, Foreign Minister Peters) decided in Sept 2025 not to recognise Palestine "yet", calling recognition inevitable but premature while Hamas remains.

labour.evidence: "Labour will recognise the State of Palestine" and place economic sanctions on Israel.

green.evidence: Recognise Palestine as a state and sanction Israel.

nz-first.evidence: Winston Peters announced at the UN in Sept 2025: "we do not think that time is now."

alliance.evidence: "We must demand self-determination for Palestinians and the right to return to their homeland."

free-palestine.evidence: Party exists to press NZ to "uphold its obligations under international law with respect to Palestine"; seeks a single democratic state.

statements.text: Defence spending should rise substantially, towards 2% of GDP.
statements.explainer: Defence spending is currently about 1% of national income. Doubling it over a decade means billions more for ships, aircraft and personnel, and less for other priorities, in return for a stronger military and closer alignment with allies.

national.evidence: National-led government's Defence Capability Plan targets 2% of GDP by 2032/33; Defence Minister Chris Penk reaffirmed "a smooth and steady upward trajectory to 2 percent" in May 2026.

green.evidence: Security policy prioritises peacekeeping and "prevention over military force" and would withdraw NZ from the Five Eyes network; no increase in military spending proposed.

act.evidence: ACT's 2026 Fiscal Plan cuts non-frontline spending but protects "the spending growth since 2017 in core frontline services such as health, education, defence" (no specific 2% target found in its 2026 documents).

te-pati-maori.evidence: Declare NZ a "military neutral" country and focus the Defence Force on protection, disaster response and the Pacific.

alliance.evidence: A "peace-focused defence force", non-alignment and an end to intelligence sharing with the US.

free-palestine.evidence: NZ should withdraw "from any formal security alliances with the U.S." and distance itself from "military interventionism".

statements.text: New Zealand should increase its overseas aid budget.
statements.explainer: Aid is about a quarter to a third of a percent of national income; the UN target is 0.7%. More aid supports Pacific neighbours and global standing; opponents say money should stay at home while there are needs here.

labour.evidence: Increase foreign aid to 0.7 percent of GDP.

green.evidence: Increase climate aid funding to the Pacific.

act.evidence: Reduce NZ's foreign aid to 2017 levels.

alliance.evidence: Developed nations should cancel Global South debts "as a form of reparation".

statements.text: Cannabis should be legalised or decriminalised for personal use.
statements.explainer: Possession is currently a crime, though police mostly use discretion. Legalising or decriminalising would end convictions for personal use and could be taxed and regulated; opponents point to health harms and youth use. A 2020 referendum narrowly rejected legalisation.

green.evidence: Decriminalise cannabis for personal use; long-term policy is a legal, regulated cannabis market.

opportunity.evidence: Decriminalise drug possession (but not supply).

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: "We do not believe cultivation or possession of cannabis for personal use should be a criminal offense."

legalise-cannabis.evidence: "That the possession, cultivation and use of pure cannabis... be free from prosecution" and a regulated R18 cannabis market.

statements.text: Children under 16 should be banned from social media.
statements.explainer: A ban would require platforms to verify ages and remove young users. Supporters cite mental health and online harm; opponents cite privacy risks of age checks, the practicality of enforcing it and parents' right to decide.

national.evidence: Ban under-16 year olds from social media (Online Safety (Minimum Age...) Bill).

labour.evidence: Backed the bill to pass its first reading and go to select committee, wanting it "substantially improved".

act.evidence: Will vote against: "The ban they propose won't work, and the side effects will leave us worse off" (David Seymour).

nz-first.evidence: Winston Peters said NZ First would "never support this", citing a slippery slope.

opportunity.evidence: Support the online safety bill on an under-16 ban going to select committee.

statements.text: Puberty blockers and other medical gender-transition treatments should not be available to people under 18.
statements.explainer: Puberty blockers delay physical changes for young people with gender dysphoria. Restricting them follows some other countries' caution over evidence; opponents say the decision should rest with young people, families and doctors.

national.evidence: Health Minister Simeon Brown halted new puberty-blocker prescriptions for gender dysphoria from 19 Dec 2025 as a "precautionary approach".

green.evidence: Free access to gender-affirming health care "including reversal of the ban on puberty blockers".

nz-first.evidence: Campaigned for the ban and announced it ahead of the Ministry; Peters: "we never stopped fighting to make this happen."

conservative.evidence: Restrict irreversible procedures to alter a child's sex characteristics "where there is no clear medical necessity" and require independent assessment.

womens-rights.evidence: Supports the puberty-blocker ban and would extend it to cross-sex hormones for under-18s and surgery for under-25s.

vision-nz.evidence: "Prohibit all medical interventions for gender transition in minors."

statements.text: Abortion law should be made more restrictive.
statements.explainer: Abortion was removed from the Crimes Act in 2020 and is available on request up to 20 weeks, with conditions after that. More restriction means tighter time limits or extra requirements; most parties treat this as a conscience issue rather than party policy.

conservative.evidence: Introduce an Unborn Child (Legal Personhood and Rights) Act recognising an unborn child as a legal person from the third trimester (28 weeks).

womens-rights.evidence: Lists "the right to have control of our own bodies, including reproductive autonomy" among the rights it exists to protect.

vision-nz.evidence: Healthcare policy commits to "protecting the sanctity of human life" (no specific abortion law change stated).

howtovote._about: How to vote in the 7 November 2026 New Zealand general election. Plain-English guide for Ballot Book NZ. Every fact is tied to the Electoral Commission page (vote.nz / elections.nz), the Act, or the news report it came from, with the date the source was retrieved. Commission pages were fetched with a headless browser on 23 October 2026 (copies in raw/howtovote/). Where a fact could not be verified against a primary source, the text says so. This guide is not legal advice: if your situation is unusual, call the Electoral Commission on 0800 36 76 56.

election.name: 2026 General Election
election.election_day_text: Saturday 7 November 2026, voting places open 9am to 7pm
election.law_change_note: In December 2025 Parliament passed the Electoral Amendment Act 2025, which (Public Act 2025 No 82, Royal assent 19 December 2025, most of it in force from 20 December 2025). It closes enrolment 13 days before election day, so there is no enrolling at a voting place during advance voting or on election day; sets a 12-day advance voting period; and bars more sentenced prisoners from voting. Sources: Ministry of Justice summary (justice.govt.nz, retrieved 23 Oct 2026); RNZ, 'Electoral Amendment Bill passes its third reading in Parliament' (Dec 2025); Electoral Act 1993 as at 1 January 2026, s 3(1) 'close of registration', s 80, s 171B.

key_dates.event: Last day for Māori already enrolled to change between the Māori roll and the general roll (midnight). You can't change rolls in the 3 months before an election.
Writ Day. If you were enrolled by this date you get an EasyVote card and are on the printed roll. Anyone who enrols or updates after this date casts a special vote.
Registration opens for telephone dictation voting (0800 028 028, option 1).
EasyVote cards start going out by email and post (delivery 14 to 22 October).
Last recommended day to post a paper enrolment form (Tuesday). Forms arriving by post after Tuesday 27 October cannot be accepted.
Overseas voting and telephone dictation voting start (Wednesday).
ENROLMENT CLOSES at midnight (Sunday). This is the last moment to enrol or update your address. No enrolling at voting places this election.
Advance voting starts in New Zealand (Monday, Labour Day). Hours vary by place. 207 voting places open on the first day.
Last day of advance voting (Friday). Regulated period for election advertising ends; all election advertising must stop and signs come down by midnight.

ELECTION DAY (Saturday). Voting places open 9am to 7pm. Telephone dictation registration closes at noon; dictation voting, overseas uploads and all voting close at 7pm NZ time. Preliminary results from 7pm on electionresults.govt.nz.
Official results declared (Friday), after special votes are checked and counted and every vote is recounted.
Last day for the return of the writ (the formal list of elected electorate MPs). The new Parliament's three-year term runs from this date.
Latest date Parliament must meet (6 weeks after the day fixed for the return of the writ, Constitution Act 1986 s 19). RNZ's The House gives the date as 14 January.

contacts.electoral_commission_freephone: 0800 36 76 56 (free, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week; enrolment questions, finding a voting place, help to vote)
contacts.text_for_an_enrolment_form: Text your name and address to 3676 (free) and a form is posted to you
contacts.enrolment_email: enrol@vote.nz (to return a scanned or photographed enrolment form)
contacts.enrol_or_check_online: https://vote.nz/enrolling/enrol-or-update/enrol-or-update-online (needs a NZ driver licence, NZ passport or RealMe verified identity)
contacts.post: Electoral Commission, FREEPOST 2 ENROL, PO Box 190, Wellington 6140
contacts.general_enquiries_email: enquiries@elections.govt.nz (questions, complaints about election advertising or misleading voting information)
contacts.telephone_dictation: 0800 028 028 within NZ (option 1 to register, option 2 to vote); +64 4 471 2000 from overseas
contacts.electorate_managers: https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/contact-your-electorate-manager (name, email and phone for each electorate; use this if you can't get to a voting place)

checklist.done_when: You are 18 or older on election day, a NZ citizen or a resident for electoral purposes (your visa doesn't make you leave by a set date), and you have lived in NZ continuously for 12 months or more at some time in your life. If you are 17 now but turn 18 by 7 November, you can enrol.

checklist.step: Check you are enrolled at your current address, before midnight Sunday 25 October
checklist.done_when: The online check at vote.nz shows your name and current address (you need a NZ driver licence, NZ passport or RealMe), or you have called 0800 36 76 56 and been told you are enrolled. After midnight 25 October nothing can be changed and you cannot enrol at a voting place.

checklist.step: Pick where and when you will vote
checklist.done_when: You have looked up a voting place and its hours on the official map (hours vary before election day), or you know a place that is open 9am to 7pm on Saturday 7 November. You can vote at any voting place in NZ, but it is quicker close to home.

checklist.step: Know what to bring: nothing is required
checklist.done_when: You know no ID is needed. If you have an EasyVote card (sent to everyone enrolled by 4 October, by email or post) bring it on paper, on your phone or as a screenshot; it makes finding you on the roll faster.

You know you make one tick on the left for a party (party vote) and one tick on the right for a local candidate (electorate vote). One tick for each. You may do just one side if you want. If you make a mistake, ask for a new paper.

checklist.step: Plan ahead if you will be away or overseas
checklist.done_when: Away from home in NZ: you know you can vote at any voting place (you will fill in a short special-vote declaration). Overseas on or after 21 October: you know you must be enrolled by 25 October, then download your papers at vote.nz/overseas, sign the declaration with a witness, and upload by 7pm NZ time on 7 November.

checklist.step: Get help if you need it
checklist.done_when: You know a friend, family member or voting place worker can go behind the screen with you, read the paper and mark it as you ask (they can't tell you who to vote for). If you are blind, have low vision or a physical disability, you have registered for telephone dictation voting (0800 028 028) by noon on 7 November. If you can't get to a voting place, you have called 0800 36 76 56 or your electorate manager.

voting_places.deep_link_notes: The official finder (map.vote.nz, redirects to map.vote.nz/voting-places) is a client-side map. It loads the whole 2026 voting-place dataset into the browser and filters it there, with an address search box (Mapbox geocoding) and filters for day, 'open now', accessibility, Whare Pōti Māori and reo rua. It takes no documented URL parameters: on 23 Oct 2026 we tested https://map.vote.nz/voting-places?electorate=Wellington%20Central and the page loaded the default view. The vote.nz list page lets you pick an electorate and suburb from drop-downs, also client-side. So the app should deep-link to https://map.vote.nz and let the voter type their address, or call 0800 36 76 56. Posters listing nearby voting places are also displayed at local supermarkets and community libraries during advance voting.
voting_places.data_endpoint: https://map.vote.nz/assets/map-data/locations-<hash>.json (the hash changes when the data is updated; on 23 Oct 2026 it was a 1.05 MB JSON file with 2,641 locations, each with name, address, suburb, WGS84 coordinates, accessibility code (none/partial/full), Whare Pōti Māori and reo rua flags, per-day opening hours, and the electorates it serves as a 'Home' or 'Shared' place). It is served from behind the Commission's bot protection (Incapsula) and is not published on data.govt.nz.
voting_places.licence: No licence statement was found on the data file, on map.vote.nz, or on vote.nz/elections.nz (their footers say only 'Copyright © Electoral Commission New Zealand'). Because there is no licence allowing reuse, the dataset is NOT stored in this repository; only the deep-link above is published. tools/howtovote_voting_places.py can normalise the file if the Commission confirms reuse terms (enquiries@elections.govt.nz). For 2023 the Commission published a 'voting place coordinates' CSV on the results archive (archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/statistics/) marked 'approximate only', again with no licence stated.
voting_places.when_published: The Commission announced the 2026 voting places on 7 October 2026 ('about 3 weeks before election day' is its stated practice). Hours and places can still change, so always check the finder before travelling.

counts_from_commission.fact: More than 2,300 voting places open on election day (the finder data held 2,314 on 23 Oct); 207 open on Monday 26 October (finder data: 209) offering 1,437 hours of voting; the number grows towards election day.

1,679 fully accessible voting places; NZ Sign Language interpreters at six locations; three voting places with quiet times; more than 220 Whare Pōti Māori voting places (marae, kura, wānanga and community spaces), including 67 bilingual (reo rua) places where you can vote in te reo Māori or English.
Votes will be taken at 2,638 locations across the whole voting period (RNZ, citing the Commission).

sections.title: 1. Am I allowed to vote?
who_its_for: people in prison or on remand

steps.text: You can enrol and vote if all three are true: you are 18 or older; you are a New Zealand citizen or a 'resident for electoral purposes'; and you have lived in New Zealand continuously for 12 months or more at some time in your life.
steps.source: vote.nz, 'Are you eligible to enrol and vote?', retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act 1993 s 74

steps.text: 'Resident for electoral purposes' means you live in New Zealand lawfully and your visa does not make you leave by a set date. Resident-visa holders (including the 2021 Resident Visa) qualify. People on work, student or visitor visas with an end date do not.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: If you are 17 you can fill in the form now. You are enrolled automatically on your 18th birthday. If you turn 18 on or before 7 November 2026, you can vote, as long as you applied to enrol by midnight 25 October.
steps.source: vote.nz EasyVote page and eligibility page, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: If you live in New Zealand and are eligible, enrolling is compulsory by law. Voting itself is not compulsory.
steps.source: vote.nz, 'Need help to vote?' (dementia section) and 'Facts about New Zealand elections', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Prison (changed in 2025): you cannot vote if you are serving a sentence of 3 years or more. You also cannot vote if you are serving a sentence of less than 3 years for any offence committed on or after 20 December 2025. You CAN still vote if you are serving less than 3 years and all your offences happened before 20 December 2025, or if you are on remand, home detention or a community sentence. The Commission works with Corrections to provide voting for eligible prisoners.
steps.source: vote.nz eligibility page, retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act 1993 s 80(1)(d) as at 1 Jan 2026 (raw/howtovote/electoral-act-1993-2026-01-01.pdf); Ministry of Justice, 'Electoral law changes'

steps.text: You also cannot vote if you are a NZ citizen who has not been in New Zealand in the last 3 years, a resident (non-citizen) who has not been in NZ in the last 12 months, if you have been held in a psychiatric hospital for more than 3 years after a criminal charge, or if you are on the Corrupt Practices List.
steps.source: vote.nz eligibility page, retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act s 80

steps.text: Homeless? You can enrol at the address where you spend most of your time, or the last address where you lived for a month or more. You need a postal address (a PO Box or a friend, family member, church or support group who will hold mail for you).
steps.source: vote.nz eligibility page, retrieved 2026-10-23

notes: The brief said 'prisoners now barred under the 2025 Act'. Verified with a correction: the ban is not total. Sentenced prisoners serving under 3 years can still vote if all their offences were before 20 December 2025 (Electoral Act s 80(1)(d)(i)-(ii); vote.nz). RNZ (Dec 2025) reported the Act 'bans prisoners from voting'; 1News (16 Oct 2026) called it 'a total ban on prisoner voting for prisoners sentenced after December 2025'. The Act's wording turns on when the offence happened, not the sentencing date.
Unsure? Call 0800 36 76 56. The law is Electoral Act 1993 ss 74 and 80.

sections.title: 2. Enrol or update your details by midnight, Sunday 25 October

steps.text: Deadline: midnight, Sunday 25 October 2026. The law now closes the roll 13 days before election day. You cannot enrol or change your address after this, and you cannot enrol at a voting place during advance voting or on election day. Voting place staff can't make exceptions; the rule is set by law.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What to do' and eligibility pages, retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act s 3(1) 'close of registration' (inserted by Electoral Amendment Act 2025 s 4(2)); 1News 16 Oct 2026 ('there are no exceptions, the Electoral Commission says')

steps.text: Fastest way: online at vote.nz with your NZ driver licence, NZ passport or RealMe verified identity. The same page lets you check what address you are enrolled at.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Commission release 22 Oct 2026

steps.text: No ID? Fill in the form online and have it emailed or posted to you to sign ('Enrol without ID' / 'Update without ID'), download the PDF form, call 0800 36 76 56, or text your name and address to 3676. Then return the signed form by upload (vote.nz/upload), email (enrol@vote.nz), or drop it at an enrolment hub. Hub times and places are at vote.nz/enrolling/get-help-to-enrol/enrolment-in-your-community.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Other ways to enrol', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Post is slow: the Commission recommended posting forms by Tuesday 20 October. It will accept forms that arrive by post on Tuesday 27 October but not after. If you still have a paper form, upload or email it, or take it to a hub.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Other ways to enrol', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Moved house but still enrolled at an old address? You can still vote, but you may need to cast a special vote. If your new home is in a different electorate, only your party vote will count. Update your address by 25 October so both votes count.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Enrol by 25 October', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Dormant roll: if mail from the Commission came back from your old address you may be on the 'dormant roll'. You can still vote (as a special vote) but, again, if you have moved electorate only your party vote counts. Updating your address before 25 October fixes this.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Not enrolled at any address by midnight 25 October? The Commission says you will not be able to vote in this election. If you turn up believing you are enrolled, you can cast a special vote, but it will be disallowed if you turn out not to be enrolled.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Enrol by 25 October', retrieved 2026-10-23; 1News 16 Oct 2026

steps.text: Unpublished roll: if you fear for your safety, you can ask to go on the confidential unpublished roll (download the form or call 0800 36 76 56). Your details are kept off printed rolls. You will then cast a special vote, you can't check or update your details online, and you can't download overseas voting papers.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Māori roll or general roll: if you are of Māori descent you choose a roll when you first enrol. You vote for the same parties on either roll; the difference is which electorate candidates you choose from. Already-enrolled Māori could change rolls until midnight 6 August 2026; the 3-month pre-election freeze now applies. If you are enrolling for the first time you can still choose either roll up to 25 October.
steps.source: vote.nz key dates and 'Māori roll or general roll?'; Electoral Commission release '17,000 Māori voters change rolls', 18 Aug 2026

notes: Why it changed: the Government said late enrolments put 'too much strain on the system' and slowed the count (Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith, quoted by RNZ, July 2025). The Attorney-General reported the cut-off 'appears to constitute an unjustified limit' on the right to vote under the Bill of Rights Act (reported by RNZ). The Chief Electoral Officer told MPs the change was 'not a change that we recommended' and would not make official results faster than 20 days (RNZ, Sept 2025). Labour has said it would reverse the change (RNZ). Both sides' views are reported here; the guide takes no position.

Scale: in 2023, about 450,000 people enrolled or updated in the final two weeks, including about 110,000 on election day (1News, 16 Oct 2026, citing Commission data). The Commission expects about 55,000 special votes to be disallowed this year, five times more than usual, because the voter turns out not to be enrolled (1News).
On 21 October 2026, 3,729,667 people were enrolled, 92.1% of those eligible; only 68.6% of 18 to 24 year olds were enrolled (Electoral Commission, 22 Oct 2026).

Enrolment packs were posted 17 to 22 August 2026; if you didn't get one, your address was out of date or you were not enrolled (Electoral Commission, 10 Aug 2026). The Commission also used data matching with NZTA and Internal Affairs to contact 170,000 people in September (release 17 Sep 2026).

sections.title: 3. When and where to vote

steps.text: Advance voting: Monday 26 October to Friday 6 November. You can vote at any voting place in New Zealand. Days and hours differ from place to place, and some places open only before election day or only on election day, so check before you go.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Find a voting place', retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act s 171B (12-day advance period)

steps.text: Election day: Saturday 7 November, every voting place open 9am to 7pm. If you are inside a voting place at 7pm waiting to vote, you can still vote.
steps.source: vote.nz key dates; Electoral Act s 161

steps.text: Find a place: use the official map at map.vote.nz (search your address; filter by day, 'open now', accessibility, Whare Pōti Māori, reo rua), the list by electorate and suburb on vote.nz, posters at your local supermarket or library, or call 0800 36 76 56.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Find a voting place'; Electoral Commission releases 7 and 22 Oct 2026

steps.text: Vote close to home if you can. It is faster because your name is on the printed roll there. Anywhere else you can still vote, but you fill in a special-vote declaration first.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What to do', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: What to bring: nothing. No ID is needed. Bring your EasyVote card if you have one (paper, phone or screenshot); it helps staff find you on the roll. You can vote without it.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Facts about New Zealand elections' ('No ID is required') and EasyVote page, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: EasyVote cards went to everyone enrolled by 4 October, by email (from no-reply@easy.vote.nz; follow-up texts from 5101) or by post, between 14 and 22 October. Check your spam folder. If you enrolled after 4 October you won't get one, but you can still vote.
steps.source: Electoral Commission release, 14 Oct 2026; vote.nz EasyVote page

steps.text: Quieter times: if you prefer less crowding or need assistance, the Commission says 9am to 11am and 2pm to 4pm on weekdays are usually best.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Need help to vote?', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Time off work on election day: if you haven't had a reasonable chance to vote before starting work, your employer must let you leave by 3pm for the rest of the day, with no pay docked. If you do essential work after 3pm, you get a reasonable time off earlier in the day, with up to 2 hours paid. Employers who refuse can be fined up to $1,000.
steps.source: Electoral Act 1993 s 162 (verified in the consolidated Act as at 1 Jan 2026, raw/howtovote/electoral-act-1993-2026-01-01.pdf); vote.nz 'Can't get to a voting place?' (time away from work section)

notes: Staff wear orange vests and will guide you. Many are working their first election; the Commission asks for patience if there are delays (vote.nz, 'What to expect at the voting place').
Monday 26 October is Labour Day; 207 voting places open that day (Commission release 22 Oct 2026; RNZ explainer 23 Oct 2026).

sections.title: 4. Voting away from home, special votes, and voting when you can't get to a voting place
who_its_for: students and workers away from home
people on the unpublished or dormant roll
people in hospital, care homes or prison
people with illness or mobility problems

steps.text: A special vote is a normal vote plus a short declaration form you sign. You cast one if your name is not on the printed roll where you vote: because you enrolled or updated after Writ Day (4 October), you are voting outside your electorate, you are on the unpublished roll, you are on the dormant roll, or you are voting from overseas or away from a voting place.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What to do'; elections.nz 'How are general election votes counted?'; Electoral Act s 61

steps.text: Voting in another electorate: you get the ballot paper for YOUR home electorate, so your electorate vote still counts, as long as you are enrolled there. If you vote for an electorate you are not enrolled in, the electorate vote is disallowed and only your party vote is counted ('Party Vote Only').
steps.source: elections.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: How special votes are counted: they are sent back to your home electorate, every declaration is checked against the roll, and they are added to the official count. They can arrive up to 10 days after election day. That is why they are not in election-night results and why official results take until 27 November.
steps.source: elections.nz; vote.nz 'What happens after an election?'

steps.text: Can't get to a voting place (illness, mobility)? Someone can collect your voting papers for you ('takeaway' voting). Sign a written authorisation (form on vote.nz, or handwritten with your name, phone, enrolled address, which roll you are on, and a line authorising the bearer). They bring the papers to you; you complete them with a witnessed special-vote declaration; they must be back at a voting place before 7pm on 7 November.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Can't get to a voting place?', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Nobody to collect them? Contact your electorate manager (list on vote.nz). It may be possible for papers to be delivered to you and collected again.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: In hospital: a friend or family member can bring you your voting papers. If you know you will be in hospital, the Commission suggests voting in advance. In a care home or rest home: you don't need to do anything; the electorate manager arranges voting with your home's manager. Ask your home what has been arranged.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Blind, low vision or a physical disability that stops you marking the paper: use telephone dictation voting (see Accessibility section). Remote locations (DOC islands, offshore installations, vessels in NZ waters): apply early to remote@vote.nz.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Remote voting', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: In prison or on remand and eligible? The Commission works with Corrections to provide voting services.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

notes: The Commission forecast around 700,000 special votes for 2026 (Chief Electoral Officer to the Justice Committee, RNZ, Sept 2025). In 2023 there were 603,257 special votes, 20.9% of all votes (Commission, 3 Nov 2023).

'Voting from home' in the sense of postal voting for everyone does not exist for general elections in New Zealand; the options above (collected papers, electorate-manager delivery, dictation, remote and overseas services) are what the Commission offers.

sections.title: 5. Voting from overseas
who_its_for: Defence Force and public servants posted overseas

steps.text: Who can: you must be enrolled, 18+, have lived in NZ for 12+ continuous months at some time, and be either a NZ citizen who has been in NZ within the last 3 years, or a resident for electoral purposes who has been in NZ within the last 12 months. Public servants, diplomats and Defence Force members posted overseas, and their families, qualify however long they have been away. Enrolling from overseas is optional.
steps.source: vote.nz 'How to vote from overseas', retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act s 80(1)(a)-(b)

steps.text: Enrol or update by midnight Sunday 25 October, NZ time. You can't download papers until your enrolment is processed, so do it early. Your electorate is where you last lived for a month or more. If you have been away too long to update online, email overseas@vote.nz.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Voting opened Wednesday 21 October (NZ time). The easiest way: download your papers at vote.nz/overseas (a 3-page PDF: instructions, declaration, ballot paper), mark them on screen or print and mark by hand, then upload them. You must be physically outside New Zealand when you download; if you download while still in NZ your vote will not be counted.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Downloading your voting papers' and 'Common questions', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: The declaration must be signed by you AND a witness who is physically with you. Typed signatures and handwriting-style fonts are not accepted; draw or insert an image of your real signature. Tick your reason for a special vote (e.g. outside NZ on election day). Your witness can be a relative, flatmate, colleague or associate, any registered NZ elector, or an official such as a notary.
steps.source: vote.nz 'How to complete your voting papers' and 'Common questions', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Upload at uvp.elections.govt.nz by 7pm on Saturday 7 November, NZ time. Late papers cannot be accepted. Upload once only: more than one submission may mean your vote doesn't count. Files: JPG, PNG, GIF, PDF or TIFF, 10 KB to 10 MB, whole page visible including the 7-digit number top right.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Uploading your voting papers', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: In person: 64 overseas locations offer in-person or postal voting, including 10 in Australia. Hours and closing dates differ, some are appointment-only or postal-only, most are closed at weekends, and ALL overseas voting places are closed on election day, 7 November. Check the lookup before you go.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Find an overseas voting place'; Electoral Commission release 21 Oct 2026

steps.text: On the unpublished roll? You can't download papers. Ask your nearest overseas voting place for a postal vote or collect papers in person, or email overseas@vote.nz.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Common questions', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Help: overseas@vote.nz or +64 9 909 4182. Blind or disabled voters overseas can use telephone dictation voting on +64 4 471 2000 (register first).
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

notes: In 2023, 88% of overseas voters used the download service; 77,295 overseas votes were received (62,787 in 2020). About 126,000 enrolled voters have told the Commission they live overseas, 64% of them in Australia (Electoral Commission, 21 Oct 2026).
Niueans, Tokelauans and Cook Islanders vote on the citizen rule (in NZ within 3 years); Australians on the resident rule (within 12 months) (vote.nz 'How to vote from overseas').
The brief's 'from 21 Oct?' is confirmed: overseas voting started Wednesday 21 October 2026 (vote.nz key dates; Commission release 21 Oct 2026).

sections.title: 6. Help to vote and accessible voting
who_its_for: people with dementia or cognitive impairment

steps.text: A support person: a friend, family member or voting place worker can go behind the screen with you, read out the paper, and mark it as you ask. They cannot tell you who to vote for. The choice must be yours and you must be present. Nobody can vote for you, not even with power of attorney.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Need help to vote?', retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act s 170

steps.text: Telephone dictation voting is for people who are blind, partially blind or have a physical disability that stops them marking the paper. You must register every election, even if you used it before. Register from Monday 5 October to noon on Saturday 7 November by calling 0800 028 028 (option 1) or +64 4 471 2000 from overseas. Registration hours: weekdays 9am to 7pm; from 26 October also Saturdays 9am to 3pm; election day 9am to noon.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Telephone dictation voting', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Then vote by phone from Wednesday 21 October to 7pm on Saturday 7 November (0800 028 028, option 2). You give your registration number and the answer to a secret question, not your name. One official reads out the candidates and parties and marks your paper; a second official checks it back with you. Dictation voting hours: weekdays 9am to 7pm, Saturdays 9am to 3pm (from 26 Oct), election day 9am to 7pm.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Commission release 21 Oct 2026

steps.text: Accessible voting places: 1,679 are fully accessible; NZSL interpreters are at six locations; three places have quiet times. The map at map.vote.nz can be filtered by accessibility.
steps.source: Electoral Commission release 7 Oct 2026; vote.nz 'Find a voting place'

steps.text: Information in other formats: audio, Braille, large print, Easy Read and New Zealand Sign Language (NZSL) versions of the enrolling and voting guides are at vote.nz. Easy Read: 'Get ready to enrol and vote in the 2026 General Election' (PDF). Most vote.nz pages also have te reo Māori and NZSL versions (language toggle at the top).
steps.source: vote.nz 'Information in accessible formats' and 'Information in Easy Read', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Access 2026 is the Commission's accessibility action plan: 20 accessible services for Deaf and disabled people, tāngata Turi (Deaf Māori) and tāngata whaikaha Māori (disabled Māori), with Easy Read, large print, audio and Braille summaries.
steps.source: Electoral Commission release 7 Sep 2026; elections.nz Access 2026 page, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Dementia or cognitive impairment: there is no capacity test for voting. A person can vote if they want to and can clearly show their choice at the time; a support person must follow their instructions.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Te reo Māori: 67 bilingual (reo rua) voting places let you vote in te reo Māori or English; more than 220 Whare Pōti Māori places are at marae, kura, wānanga and community spaces. Filter the map for 'Whare Pōti Māori' and 'Reo rua'.
steps.source: Electoral Commission release 7 Oct 2026

notes: Quiet times at voting places are generally 9am to 11am and 2pm to 4pm on weekdays (vote.nz).

The Access 2026 'Quick guide to accessible voting services' PDF could not be downloaded (bot protection); its contents are summarised from the Access 2026 web page and the telephone dictation page instead.
Disabled voters told 1News (5 Oct 2026, cited in docs/FEATURE_REVIEW.md) they were still hunting for accessible booths; the map's accessibility filter and 0800 36 76 56 are the Commission's answers.

sections.title: 7. First time voting? What happens inside, and the two ticks

steps.text: Arrive. Staff in orange vests greet you. Give your EasyVote card, or your name and address, to the person issuing papers. They find you on the roll (electronic roll for dormant-roll voters) and hand you your voting paper. If you are not on the printed roll you fill in a special-vote declaration first.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What to expect' and 'What to do', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Go to a voting screen and vote in private, with a pen. You get two votes on one paper. LEFT side: your party vote. Tick ONE circle next to the party you want in government. RIGHT side: your electorate vote. Tick ONE circle next to the candidate you want as the MP for your area.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What to do', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: You can tick both sides, or just one side. Both are valid. The party vote decides how many seats each party gets in Parliament; the electorate vote picks your local MP. Your EasyVote card comes with the list of candidates for your electorate; party lists are on vote.nz.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What to do' ('vote for only one or the other, it's your choice'); elections.nz 'What happens in a general election?'

steps.text: Made a mistake? Take the 'spoilt' paper back and ask for a new one. Spoilt papers are not counted. An 'informal' vote is one where the counters cannot tell what you intended; it is recorded but does not count. If your intention is clear, your vote counts even if the paper has been drawn on.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What to do' (spoilt papers) and 'Facts about New Zealand elections' (informal votes), retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Fold the paper in half and put it in the ballot box. Then leave; the Commission asks voters not to linger so others feel comfortable.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What to do' and 'What to expect', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Phones and selfies: don't film or photograph inside a voting place. Publishing a photo or video of someone filling in their paper is a potential offence. Candidates who want to be filmed voting must arrange it in advance (returns@elections.govt.nz / the Returning Officer).
steps.source: vote.nz 'What to expect'; Electoral Commission, 'Rules once voting starts and on election day' (PDF, 2026)

steps.text: Campaigning near voting places: during advance voting, no campaigning, election advertising or influencing voters inside a voting place or within 10 metres of its entrance. On election day those rules apply everywhere until 7pm: no campaign material (a lapel badge or rosette is allowed), no processions, no polling voters. New in 2026: nobody may give out free food, drink (except water) or entertainment within 100 metres of a voting place entrance while voting is open, unless it is their normal business.
steps.source: Electoral Commission, 'Rules once voting starts and on election day' (raw/howtovote/rules-once-voting-starts.pdf); Ministry of Justice summary of the 2025 Act

steps.text: Social media on election day: from midnight before election day until 7pm on 7 November, you must not post or share anything likely to influence someone's party or candidate vote. There is no exemption for personal opinions online on election day. Posts made before election day can stay up if not updated. Paid election advertising online is banned on election day.
steps.source: elections.nz 'Social media' and vote.nz 'What to expect', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Scrutineers: you may see people with party rosettes sitting along one side. They are appointed by candidates and parties to watch, not Commission staff, and they cannot talk to voters.
steps.source: vote.nz 'Facts about New Zealand elections', retrieved 2026-10-23

notes: Votes are counted by hand; New Zealand does not use voting machines (vote.nz, 'Facts about New Zealand elections').

Who to vote for is your decision. This guide does not recommend anyone. RNZ's 23 Oct 2026 explainer points first-time voters to non-partisan candidate information at policy.nz and the parties' own websites.

If you vote for an electorate you are not enrolled in (e.g. you moved and didn't update), only your party vote counts (elections.nz, 'Party Vote Only'). In 2023 more than 42,000 electorate votes were disallowed for this reason; the Commission estimated more than 72,000 could be this year (1News, 16 Oct 2026).

sections.title: 8. After you vote: results and forming a government

steps.text: Election night: advance votes are counted from 9am on election day at electorate headquarters; election-day votes are counted at each voting place after 7pm. Preliminary results go up progressively from 7pm on electionresults.govt.nz. The Commission's targets: 50% of results by 10pm and 95% by 11.30pm.
steps.source: elections.nz 'How are general election votes counted?'; vote.nz 'What happens after an election?', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Election-night results are NOT final. They leave out all special votes (including overseas votes) and the rolls have not yet been checked. The Commission says they 'are likely to change'.
steps.source: vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Special votes have changed results before. 2023: after specials, National went from 50 seats to 48, Te Pāti Māori from 4 to 6, the Greens from 14 to 15; Nelson, Te Atatū, Tāmaki Makaurau (by 4 votes) and Te Tai Tokerau changed hands; National and ACT alone no longer had a majority. 603,257 special votes were 20.9% of the total.
steps.source: Electoral Commission, 'Official results for the 2023 General Election', 3 Nov 2023

steps.text: 2020: National fell from 35 seats to 33, Labour rose from 64 to 65 and the Māori Party from 1 to 2; Maungakiekie, Northland and Whangārei switched from National to Labour. 504,625 special votes were 17% of the total.
steps.source: Electoral Commission, '2020 General Election official results', 6 Nov 2020

steps.text: Official results: Friday 27 November 2026 (20 days after election day). Every vote is recounted by hand, special votes (which can arrive up to 10 days after election day) are checked and counted, and the rolls are checked for double voting. Results are published in the NZ Gazette and on electionresults.govt.nz.
steps.source: vote.nz key dates; elections.nz 'How are general election votes counted?'

steps.text: Recounts and challenges: a candidate or party can apply for a recount within 3 working days of the official results; an election petition to the High Court must be filed within 28 days.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What happens after an election?', retrieved 2026-10-23

steps.text: Forming a government: every electorate winner gets a seat; the rest are filled from party lists in proportion to the party vote. Under MMP one party rarely wins alone, so parties negotiate a coalition or support ('confidence and supply') deal. There is no deadline for this. The outgoing government stays on as a caretaker, avoiding major decisions, until a new one is sworn in.
steps.source: vote.nz 'What happens after an election?' (Government formation); RNZ The House, 2026

steps.text: The writ is returned by 3 December 2026 with the names of elected MPs; the new Parliament's three-year term runs from that day. Parliament must meet within 6 weeks of that date (Constitution Act 1986 s 19), so by 14 January 2027 even if coalition talks are still going. The first sitting day MPs are sworn in and elect a Speaker (Commission Opening); the next day the Governor-General gives the Speech from the Throne (State Opening).
steps.source: RNZ The House (Clerk of the House David Wilson), 2026; Constitution Act 1986 ss 17 and 19 (raw/howtovote/constitution-act-1986.pdf); vote.nz key dates

notes: Why specials lean a certain way is analysis, not Commission fact: 1News (3 Nov 2023) wrote that special votes 'have historically tended to skew left'. The guide reports the shifts, not the reasons.

In 2023 the official count took three weeks; the Chief Electoral Officer told MPs in September 2025 the 2025 law change would not make the 20-day official result faster, because people enrolling between Writ Day and the 13-day close still cast special votes (RNZ).
Voting papers are kept sealed for six months in case of a legal challenge, then destroyed (vote.nz).

Parliament's and DPMC's own post-election pages (election-2026-timeline, Cabinet Office circular CO (26) 5) could not be fetched (bot protection), so government-formation steps are sourced to vote.nz, RNZ's The House and the Constitution Act.

sections.title: 9. Check before you share: official sources and where to report
who_its_for: people who see election claims on social media
